newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada may postpone some voting due to flooding.
newsitem.headline: Canada may postpone some voting due to flooding.

text.p: Canada's chief electoral officer, Jean-Pierre Kingsley, said he was flying to Manitoba on Thursday to see if severe flooding there necessitated postponing federal elections in the area.

The Reform Party on Wednesday recommended that voting be put off for up to three months in the flood area while the election proceeded in the rest of Canada. Other opposition parties agreed and Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Wednesday he would await Kingsley's recommendations.
"I have decided that it is important for me to go to Manitoba," Kingsley told a news conference on Thursday.

Television pictures broadcast across Canada showed scenes of flooding from the Red River not seen in Manitoba for 145 years. Kingsley said 10 of Manitoba's 14 electoral districts, or ridings, were potentially affected. The Liberals took 12 Manitoba seats in the last election in 1993.
Chretien called the June 2 elections on Sunday, one day after visiting the flooded area. His Liberals command a solid lead in the race for the House of Commons' 301 seats.

Reform leader Preston Manning told a news conference, referring to Manitobans: "I think the immediate thing would be to remove this item of the election off their minds right now, when they really don't want to deal with it."

Asked if this might deprive them of deciding the overall outcome, he said: "If the election ended up being close, and you were going to have nine by-elections 30 or 40 days later, it would give an enormous attention (to the Manitobans)."
Canada's Elections Act provides for the possible postponing of elections in districts affected by such things as floods or fires but this provision has never been used.
Normally Chretien, who has 174 seats now out of a slightly smaller 295-seat House of Commons, would require 151 seats to return with a majority government.

Kingsley said if elections were postponed in some Manitoba districts those seats would be considered vacant. This would presumably mean Chretien could still form a government with fewer than 151 seats until Manitoba had its say.
